title: Vayikra: the small alef (Leviticus 1:1)
hookLine: the first word is written with a small letter; midrash sees Moses' humility

lines: WRITTEN BY HAND, LETTER BY LETTER.
cards: A Torah scroll is written by hand on parchment, letter by letter, by a trained scribe. The rules are strict: every letter complete, every space the right size, and the scribe copies from a checked text, not from memory.
One wrong letter can make a scroll unfit to read in public. So when one letter is written noticeably smaller than its neighbors, it's no slip of the pen.
It's on purpose, a scribal tradition handed down from scribe to scribe. And it sits in the very first word of Leviticus.

teach.h: THE ALEF OF VAYIKRA, WRITTEN SMALL.
teach.b: The word is vayikra, and He called, and the small letter is its last one, an alef. The Torah never explains why, so the commentators asked.

The medieval commentator known as the Baal HaTurim points out that without the alef, vayikra becomes vayikar: and He happened upon, as if by chance. That's the word used when God appears to Balaam, the prophet for hire.
Moses, the story goes, was so humble he wanted to write his own call that way, as if God had only bumped into him. God told him to write the alef. So Moses wrote it, but small.

teach.h: ADAM'S BIG ALEF, MOSES' SMALL ONE.
teach.b: Another teaching sets it beside a large alef: the first letter of Adam's name, at the start of the book of Chronicles, is written big.
In that teaching, Adam, made by God's own hands, grew too sure of himself, while Moses, who spoke with God face to face, made himself small.
The Torah does call Moses humble: "Now the man Moses was very meek, above all the men that were upon the face of the earth." But notice what his humility isn't.
Moses doesn't refuse the call or leave out the letter. He goes into the tent, does the work, writes the word. He just doesn't make the letter bigger than it needs to be.
In this reading, humility means taking up the space the task needs, and no more.

how: Torah scribes write the final alef of vayikra smaller than the surrounding letters, following the scribal tradition, and printed Hebrew Bibles often reproduce it.

o: a small letter: the alef written small
and he spoke: the start of a command
and He called: Leviticus's first word

games.q: what's inside the letter — tap the pairs.
p: as if by chance, said of Balaam

s: the small alef is a copying mistake
it's a deliberate scribal tradition, kept in Torah scrolls.
the Torah explains why the alef is small
it doesn't. the reasons come from later commentators.
without the alef, vayikra reads like 'He happened upon'
vayikar, the word used when God appears to Balaam.

games.q: you're Moses, writing the word for how God called you into the tent. you'd rather not make a big deal of it. what do you do?
o: leave out the alef, so it reads 'happened upon'.
games.why: in the Baal HaTurim's telling, God wouldn't let Moses leave it out, so he wrote it small. humble, but still answering the call.

practice: Think of a place where you tend to take up a lot of room: a meeting where you talk first, a family conversation you steer, a group chat where you always have the last word.
Picture yourself there, still present and doing your part, but a little smaller: asking one question instead of making one point, letting someone else go first.

wordCard.voice: Vayikra. And He called. The first word of Leviticus, whose final alef scribes write small.

orig.note: Hebrew: alef, the first letter of the alphabet, written small at the end of vayikra.

carryVoice: Your line: the small letter. Small, but still written, and still answering. Day three hundred eighty, done.
